# Saturated empty lattice polytopes need not have width one
archived construction in
`candidate ec1a047aab7b654b`.
Its existing independent audit is
`unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
The original exact verifier was independently rerun and passed.
The seven-inequality emptiness certificate below shortens its
29-facet certificate; no classification theorem is used.

## 1. Exact counterexample

There is a full-dimensional lattice polytope Q in R^4 such that

    Q intersect Z^4 = vert(Q),
    |vert(Q)|=16=2^4,
    lattice width(Q)=2.

Let Q be the convex hull of the following points. The third column
gives an integer functional strictly exposing the corresponding
point; the last column is its minimum positive gap to all other
listed points.

| i | p_i | n_i | minimum gap |
|---|---|---|---:|
|0|(1,0,0,0)|(22,-2,-2,-8)|20|
|1|(0,1,0,0)|(2,36,-19,-4)|23|
|2|(0,0,1,0)|(4,-16,6,-2)|2|
|3|(0,0,0,1)|(-2,-2,-2,-1)|1|
|4|(2,2,3,5)|(16,10,-10,3)|15|
|5|(1,3,5,5)|(-15,17,-3,2)|13|
|6|(0,0,0,2)|(-14,-2,-16,17)|17|
|7|(1,2,4,5)|(2,-14,6,3)|3|
|8|(1,1,2,3)|(7,-24,7,4)|1|
|9|(0,1,1,1)|(-17,6,-2,3)|1|
|10|(0,1,3,2)|(-10,-7,6,2)|5|
|11|(1,2,3,4)|(-8,14,-11,7)|1|
|12|(0,1,2,1)|(3,7,5,-9)|1|
|13|(1,1,2,2)|(7,-5,6,-3)|1|
|14|(1,1,1,2)|(6,6,-11,3)|1|
|15|(1,2,3,3)|(15,15,3,-12)|3|

In precise terms the last entry is
min_{j!=i} n_i.(p_i-p_j)>0. These displayed integer dot products
certify that every p_i is a vertex. The determinant of the four
rows p_i-p_0 for i=1,2,3,4 is -11, proving full dimension.
Reduction of the sixteen listed points modulo two gives all sixteen
parity classes, each exactly once.

## 2. Seven inequalities certify emptiness

Write coordinates as (x,y,z,w). Every listed point, and hence Q,
lies in the box

    0<=x<=2, 0<=y<=3, 0<=z<=5, 0<=w<=5

and satisfies the seven integer inequalities

    3x+3y+2z-4w <= 3,
     x-6y+2z+ w <= 2,
    -3x+6y-5z+3w <= 6,
   -10x+3y- z+2w <= 4,
     2x+ y-3z+ w <= 2,
     3x-3y+3z- w <= 4,
       -x-y-z-w <= -1.                              (1)

Here is an explicit finite integer certificate for their intersection
with the box. For fixed integers x,y,z in their displayed ranges,
the allowed fourth coordinates are exactly the integers L<=w<=U,
where

    L=max(0, ceil((3x+3y+2z-3)/4),
            3x-3y+3z-4, 1-x-y-z),
    U=min(5, 2-x+6y-2z, floor((6+3x-6y+5z)/3),
            floor((4+10x-3y+z)/2), 2-2x-y+3z).

Substitution of z=0,...,5 gives this complete table:

| (x,y) | allowed (z,w) |
|---|---|
|(0,0)|(0,1), (0,2), (1,0)|
|(0,1)|(0,0), (1,1), (2,1), (3,2)|
|(0,2)|none|
|(0,3)|none|
|(1,0)|(0,0)|
|(1,1)|(1,2), (2,2), (2,3)|
|(1,2)|(3,3), (3,4), (4,5)|
|(1,3)|(5,5)|
|(2,0)|none|
|(2,1)|none|
|(2,2)|(3,5)|
|(2,3)|none|

These are exactly the sixteen p_i. Any integer point of Q must
satisfy the box and (1), and hence belongs to this list. Conversely
all listed points are in Q by definition. Thus Q intersect Z^4
is exactly its sixteen vertices. The seven inequalities need not
be a complete facet description: their validity and the displayed
integer enumeration already suffice for this conclusion.

## 3. Exact lattice width

The first coordinate has width two. Suppose a nonzero integer
functional c=(c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4) had width at most one. Its values on
integer vertices lie in {t,t+1} for an integer t. Since e_1,...,e_4
are among the vertices, c_i=t+epsilon_i with epsilon_i in {0,1}.
Its value at (2,2,3,5) then implies

    11t+2epsilon_1+2epsilon_2+3epsilon_3+5epsilon_4
        in {0,1}.                                    (2)

The subset sum lies between zero and twelve. Thus t is zero or
minus one. The subset sums of (2,2,3,5) contain neither one nor
eleven: every nonempty sum is at least two, and eleven would have
a complementary sum one. For t=0, (2) therefore forces all epsilon_i
zero; for t=-1, it forces all epsilon_i one. Both give c=0,
a contradiction. Thus every nonzero integer functional has width
at least two, and the exhibited first-coordinate functional proves
width exactly two.

## 4. It also occurs as saturated facet witnesses

The extra provenance of being relative-interior witnesses on distinct
facets of a lattice-free polyhedron does not restore width one.
Using the displayed exposing normals, set

    L={x in R^4: n_i.(x-p_i)<=0 for i=0,...,15}.        (3)

It contains the full-dimensional Q. Each p_i satisfies exactly its
own inequality at equality and every other inequality strictly.
Hence that inequality is an irredundant facet and p_i lies in its
relative interior. Thus L has exactly sixteen facets.

To prove lattice-freeness, use the already established full-parity
forest argument, included here for completeness. For any z in Z^4
let p(z) be the unique listed point with the same parity and put
R(z)=(z+p(z))/2. The orbit remains in the bounded convex hull of z
and Q, so a repeated lattice point eventually occurs. A cycle of
length k satisfies

    (2^k-1)z_0=sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^j p(z_j).

Therefore z_0 is an integer point of Q and hence a listed vertex.
Its extremality and the positive coefficients force every cycle
digit to be that same vertex. Every orbit thus terminates at some
p_s. If R^k(z)=p_s, iterating the relation gives

    z-p_s=sum_{j=0}^{k-1}2^j(p_s-p(z_j)).

For a nonroot z, at least one digit differs from p_s. Applying n_s
then gives a strictly positive value, since n_s strictly exposes
p_s among all the digits. That violates inequality s in (3).
Consequently L intersect Z^4 is exactly the sixteen p_i, all on
its boundary. It is a full-dimensional lattice-free polyhedron
with 2^4 relative-interior facet witnesses whose hull has width two.

The usual maximality conclusion can also be checked directly. For
q outside L choose a violated facet i. For sufficiently small alpha>0,
r=(p_i-alpha q)/(1-alpha) lies in int(L): its i-th inequality is
strict in the inward direction, and the other finitely many strict
inequalities persist near p_i. Since
p_i=(1-alpha)r+alpha q and r has an interior ball, p_i is interior
to conv(L,q). Thus every proper convex superset contains an integer
point in its interior, proving that L is maximal lattice-free.
This uses only relative-interior witnesses, not a classification.

## 5. Scope

This is a certified counterexample to the proposed width-one claim,
even for saturated lattice-free facet witnesses. It is not merely
a parity-complete set: emptiness and exposure were separately
certified above. It supplies no counterexample to OC. A further
argument involving original mixed-fiber cap masses or critical
circuits would need genuinely additional information beyond this
witness geometry.

The original archive verifier and the shorter independent verifier
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_saturated_empty_width_two_certificate_minkowski.py` check
the exact finite arithmetic. The forest proof is an application of
`candidate 668ad0ef7a63372e`, not a newly assumed classification.
